prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. Figure 1.4-6 Example of paving for comprehensive roads F. Smart city demonstration roads No special requirements

The setting of walkway lights and streetlights shall take the intersection stop line as the starting and ending point, at a distance of 3.0 m–10.0 m. Figure 4.3-4 Example of Walkway Lights 4.3.3 Pavement Surfacing 1. Sidewalk paving: It shall meet the requirements of stability, anti-slip performance, flatness, ecological environmental protection, and urban landscape. Its design shall be practical, economical, aesthetically pleasing, and durable, and shall be designed for permeability in accordance with sponge city requirements. Guidance and directional signs may be added to the paving; signs shall be appropriately scaled and clearly informative. 2. Tactile paving: The color of tactile paving should contrast with the color of adjacent sidewalk paving and be coordinated with the surrounding landscape. The surface of tactile paving profiles shall have anti-slip functionality. The width should be 0.3 m–0.6 m, and the tactile pattern shall protrude 4 mm above the road surface. Tactile paving shall be laid continuously and shall avoid obstacles such as trees (tree pits), utility poles, and guy wires. Figure 4.3-5 Example of tactile paving 3. Curb stones: These shall be designed in accordance with road class, construction scale, landscape environment, and usage requirements. Sidewalks must be provided with curb ramps at all intersections and at the entrances/exits of residential communities and institutions fronting the street. The height difference between the curb stone and the road surface shall not exceed 1 cm. At pedestrian crossings, the centerline of the curb-ramp opening should align with the centerline of the crosswalk. At road intersections, curb ramps are recommended to adopt a full-width, single-sided ramp descending to the bottom. 4. Tree pits / tree grates: Their dimensions shall be designed in coordination with the sidewalk paving, forming a certain proportional modular relationship. The paved surface of the tree pit / tree grate should be flush with the sidewalk paving. Tree grates should preferably use fiberglass grating, eco-friendly rubber, stone paving, and similar materials. In parks, squares, commercial pedestrian streets, and other leisure activity areas, tree pits should be designed in combination with seating, or as compact / multifunctional designs that provide seating functions. Figure 4.3-6 Example of tree pits / tree grates 5. Manhole covers: All types of manhole covers shall comply with the relevant standards in Manhole Covers (GB/T 23858-2009). The paved surface of the manhole cover shall be flush with the sidewalk paving surface, and the height difference shall not exceed 1 cm. Concealed manhole covers may be used; the decorative surface layer shall be unified with the road paving. Manhole covers with distinctive patterns may also be used. Figure 4.3-7 Example of manhole covers 4.3.4 Information service facilities Information service facilities refer to service facilities that provide information on roads, places, public announcements, and similar matters within an area. prompt_c3:
As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):
{
"scores": {
"justice": {
"overall": 68.0,
"equity": 70.0,
"fairness": 60.0,
"accessibility": 75.0
},
"safety": 72.0,
"livability": 65.0,
"sustainability": 58.0,
"aesthetics": 80.0,
"comfort": 62.0,
"walkability": 70.0
},
"explanations": {
"justice": [
"Wide sidewalks and ramps improve accessibility",
"Lack of tactile paving reduces fairness for visually impaired users",
"Sidewalk width is suitable for wheelchairs, reflecting equitable distribution"
],
"safety": [
"Separated bike lanes reduce conflict with vehicles",
"Limited visible lighting may reduce nighttime safety",
"Clear separation between sidewalk and driveway enhances walking safety"
],
"livability": [
"Ground-floor commercial units and visible activity indicate a vibrant environment",
"Proximity to convenience stores and community facilities meets daily needs",
"Pedestrian activity on the street increases community vitality"
],
"sustainability": [
"The presence of bike lanes and bus stops supports low-carbon travel",
"Low tree coverage indicates a lack of green infrastructure",
"No obvious rainwater infiltration facilities found"
],
"aesthetics": [
"Uniform building heights and consistent facade designs create visual coherence",
"High street cleanliness and well-maintained environment",
"Appropriate greenery embellishments enhance visual appeal"
],
"comfort": [
"Sparse tree coverage and lack of shading facilities may lead to thermal discomfort in hot weather",
"Lack of benches or resting points reduces comfort for elderly pedestrians",
"Wide, flat sidewalk surfaces support comfortable walking",
"Low traffic noise provides good acoustic comfort"
],
"walkability": [
"Sidewalk continuity and width support safe walking",
"Frequent crossings and curb ramps improve route connectivity",
"Street-level shade and frontage activity increase walking comfort and attractiveness"
]
}
}
 5. Quality Redlines:
1. All scores must include one decimal place.
2. Each array in explanations must contain at least 3 reasons based on specific objects in the image (e.g., benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings).
3. Analysis content must strictly match the persona setting; generic evaluations unrelated to the specified perspective are strictly prohibited.

Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Paved areas should have shading measures, and the shaded area in summer should preferably be greater than 50% of the recreational activity area. 1.4.1 Paving Style and Color 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. Figure 1.4-6 Example of paving for comprehensive roads F. Smart city demonstration roads No special requirements

Sidewalks shall be firm and level, with no ponding, no settlement, no uneven joints, and no detachment; they shall connect smoothly with adjacent structures, and the surface shall be flat and dense. The flatness of concrete precast brick pavements shall be ≤2 mm, and the flatness of stone pavements shall be ≤3 mm. 2. Sidewalk blocks shall have uniform joint widths and fully filled joints. The strength standard for paved sidewalk surfaces shall follow plaza standards; the compressive strength of concrete blocks shall be ≥35 MPa, and the flexural strength shall be ≥4.5 MPa. All manhole covers shall be flush with the sidewalk elevation and in good condition, and the strength of manhole covers must meet sidewalk traffic requirements. 3. The skid resistance of sidewalks shall meet BPN ≥60. Curbstones at the same level as the sidewalk shall likewise meet the sidewalk skid-resistance requirement of BPN ≥60. 4. When

Figure 4.3-4 Example of Walkway Lights 4.3.3 Pavement Surfacing 1. Sidewalk paving: It shall meet the requirements of stability, anti-slip performance, flatness, ecological environmental protection, and urban landscape. Its design shall be practical, economical, aesthetically pleasing, and durable, and shall be designed for permeability in accordance with sponge city requirements. Guidance and directional signs may be added to the paving; signs shall be appropriately scaled and clearly informative. 2. Tactile paving: The color of tactile paving should contrast with the color of adjacent sidewalk paving and be coordinated with the surrounding landscape. The surface of tactile paving profiles shall have anti-slip functionality. The width should be 0.3 m–0.6 m, and the tactile pattern shall protrude 4 mm above the road surface. Tactile paving shall be laid continuously and shall avoid obstacles such as trees (tree pits), utility poles, and guy wires. Figure 4.3-5 Example of tactile paving 3. Curb stones: These shall be designed in accordance with road class, construction scale, landscape environment, and usage requirements. Sidewalks must be provided with curb ramps at all intersections and at the entrances/exits of residential communities and institutions fronting the street. The height difference between the curb stone and the road surface shall not exceed 1 cm. At pedestrian crossings, the centerline of the curb-ramp opening should align with the centerline of the crosswalk. At road intersections, curb ramps are recommended to adopt a full-width, single-sided ramp descending to the bottom. 4. Tree pits / tree grates: Their dimensions shall be designed in coordination with the sidewalk paving, forming a certain proportional modular relationship. The paved surface of the tree pit / tree grate should be flush with the sidewalk paving. Tree grates should preferably use fiberglass grating, eco-friendly rubber, stone paving, and similar materials. In parks, squares, commercial pedestrian streets, and other leisure activity areas, tree pits should be designed in combination with seating, or as compact / multifunctional designs that provide seating functions. Figure 4.3-6 Example of tree pits / tree grates 5. Manhole covers: All types of manhole covers shall comply with the relevant standards in Manhole Covers (GB/T 23858-2009). The paved surface of the manhole cover shall be flush with the sidewalk paving surface, and the height difference shall not exceed 1 cm. Concealed manhole covers may be used; the decorative surface layer shall be unified with the road paving. Manhole covers with distinctive patterns may also be used.
